For me, there are only 2 things I need to take a trade: - a zone that could turn price, be it a FL, FTR, QM, whatever - a reason to enter the trade

Finding zones is what RTM is all about. The excellent analysis techniques provide us with the means to identify possible turning points ahead of time. We could just set POs, and trust that more will work than will not, which is no doubt a profitable way of trading provided you're getting at least 2 or 3R on your trades.

But if we really want to bump up our win %age, we need a good reason to enter the trade at the zone, merely apart from the fact that price has arrived there. What's a good reason? PA of course. We let the market tell us the intentions of the ITs.

What's a good type of PA to look out for? For me at least, it's the initial surge from a level that engs something significant, and then returns to source. That's where we enter.

I like to use D1/H4/H1 for my zones, and M15/M5 for my entry PA. Once you get used to spotting these types of trades, they're everywhere. Some may only make a small surge up to the next zone, some may keep going for much longer - that's when your HTF analysis comes into play.

To my mind though, I'm quite happy grabbing 3 or 4R off a good surge in 30 mins. If I want to hit the equivalent of 20R on a trade, I've got 2 options - leave it running for ages, and risk my HTF analysis being wrong, or if I'm confident in my win %age, rolling the profits of the first trade into a second. If I lose, then I'm just back to where I started for the day. If I win the second, that's getting on for some decent account gain, depending on your risk level.

I like to trade between 2 and 4% risk depending on how much I like the look of things. If I hit 3R off a 4% trade (12%), and then roll that into a second and do it again (12 x 3 = 36, plus the original 12 = 48%) then I've almost increased my account by 50% just off 2 single 3R trades, which can usually play out in an hour or less.

I've even written it down so I can see it in front of me - "3R, and then 3R, that's all you need".

Obviously you need to be quite consistent to get this to work well, which is why I use the two steps mentioned above. I'll just post a couple of quick examples so I can illustrate what I mean.

You can be in and out, with your 3/5/10/20/50% whatever, off a couple of trades in less than an hour, and then go and do something else with your day.

This method doesn't always work - sometimes you get V-shaped bottoms or tops, where price just runs away. C'est la vie, we don't need to be on every single move the market makes. I'd rather miss out on these, than risk getting 50% of them wrong by using "blind" POs at certain levels.

There are of course other tell-tale signs, such as CP into a level, etc. But for me at least, this is the most blindingly obvious PA to look out for.

Some thoughts on pinpointing good bounce levels for POs with great RR. Expect to lose a few, but pull even a couple off, and you're quids in.

The key is confluence of levels as always, which help us to identify which supply/demand levels are the important ones. I don't trade AJ unfortunately, I just loaded it up for a quick peek ahead of the open of the Asian session, and saw this.

Here's the candle body line concept in action again. I first learned of this idea a while back, when I was still in the wilderness before RTM, from a great trader on another forum, who called the concept a "zero line" (or "z line" for short), because it's quite frequently the point where breakout traders will have their trades zeroed out by a RT after they've moved their stops to B/E, before their stops are hit and add fuel to the fire, and the move continues on its way.

We can't just use them blindly, there has to exist a confluence of factors to strengthen the decision.

And of course, obviously, they do just represent a place within a supply or demand zone. But they represent a great place for us to start narrowing down our search for pinpoint trades. I've seen price bounce off them almost to the pip so many times over the time I've been trading, that it would be foolish of me not to include them in my toolkit.

Why do they work? Most of the time, if you draw them in and drop timeframe, you'll find that what has been marked is actually some local SR which held price up or down for a while before a surge, or also quite often the edge of the last LTF FTR which get's momo'd over by a surge, which then becomes an ignored SD level. Both of these things we know are usually good for a bounce.

Here's a daily chart of NU, where I've marked in some z lines and shown where price reacted to them. You can find them on any timeframe, but obviously the higher timeframe ones are more probable for big bounces.

Here's today's NU surge and drop on LTF.

When it comes down to it, it's all just boxes (FL/FTR SD zones) and lines (SR, z lines etc). Why anyone would waste time with squiqqly line indicators all over their chart is beyond me.

Playing round with a bit of volatility analysis. For the pairs I look at currently, I divided each day into 15 minute segments, and then calculated the cumulative total of each bar's range as a ratio to the average M15 ATR for that pair. Basically, I'm trying to find the best times of day to trade for quick movement.

No real surprises to be honest. Pairs with a GBP component get a nice surge around London open, USD crosses around about 1330 for 3 or 4 hours. A lot of important news tends to come out at 1330 GMT, so that'd explain the large spike around then. AUD/JPY pairs also get a nice spike around 0100, from the Asian session.

All the QMs and LTF engs in the world won't help you when you're trying to go long on something over and over again which has spiked into and fallen away from a daily FTR.

Basic supp/dem analysis fail. Not the first time I've done this either.

As I saw IF mention on another thread, the RTM material isn't a set of individual pictures - it's a collection of pieces of a jigsaw, which all must fit together in order to make sense and work well. Most of the things we learn here are in essence enhancements to basic supply and demand theory. Trying to put it all together without the underlying HTF S/D knowledge is like trying to drive a Ferrari, with nice wheels, bodywork, fat exhaust, but no engine.

I am getting a little frustrated with myself at being "nearly there" for some time now, but it's still only just over 2 months since I found RTM. I always expect a lot from myself, so I've just got to cut myself some slack, and realise it will take a little more time.

I still feel like I'm learning a lot, so once I manage to slot it all together and remember my basics primarily, I know I'll be good.

Sunday's always a good time to play around with some code. After falling afoul of losing sight of the big picture last week, I've been messing around with a good way to superimpose HTF S/D zones on top of each other, in a clear, easily visually identifiable manner. I was previously using outline boxes with borders of various thickness, but I quickly ended up with a confusing mess of lines on my chart.

As I'm sure anyone who has experimented with drawing rectangles on top of each other in MT4 knows, it's got an annoying habit of flipping colours of overlapping shapes, so that you end up with weird and wonderful shades, none of which was what you originally wanted. It's possible to apply a bitwise negation to a rectangle's colour before drawing it in order to counter this effect, but you still run into problems when one part of a rectangle overlaps another, and one part does not.

The only way I could reliably find to achieve the effect I was looking for was to convert the rectangle's price/time co-ordinates to x/y using the built in function, and then draw a rectangle label exactly on top of the original one. Rectangle labels do not suffer from the aforementioned colour flipping problem, but they are fixed in position - as you scroll the chart, they remain fixed in the same place. As such, you have to implement a timer function to redraw them every couple of hundred milliseconds in the correct position, which is a bit of a bodge (there is a lag effect as you scroll the chart quickly), but works. Also some other small caveats like making sure you sort your list of rectangles into descending order of timeframe (W1 then D1 then H4 etc) so that the correct drawing order is respected.

All a bit geeky, but I'm still a software developer at heart, and I always like trying to come up with creative solutions to work around the limitations of software. The end result is quite nice - here's a recent chart of GBPCHF, where we can see price hitting the nested H1/H4/D1/W1 supply zones, and falling off nicely.

Next up on the list is a way for me to quickly indicate which zones are engulf sources, and getting some good colours to indicate engulfed zones on various TFs. The more information I can assimilate from a single glance at a chart, the quicker I can make decisions about which direction to try and look for entries on LTF, and trade accordingly.

As an aside, this approach also lends itself quite nicely to a S/D radar, which will show me, once the zones are drawn, at a glance for all pairs I trade which ones are currently in tradeable zones.
